title: The Wrong-Person Test: 17 Checks Before Your CRM Workflow Runs Without You
subtitle: A pre-flight diagnostic for $1M-$20M marketing and creative agencies deciding which CRM workflows are safe to run fully hands-off and which still need a human approval gate.

methodology_anchor.name: Agent-Ready Ops
preconditions: Structured input data. Your CRM fields are clean enough to be the input layer for an automated decision.
Documentable decision logic. The routing rules a human follows can be written down explicitly.
Narrow initial scope. The first cut handles a single decision in a single workflow, not a sweep.
Human-in-the-loop by design. Every output that touches a client passes a person before it sends.
methodology_anchor.intro: This assessment scores your CRM workflows against the four preconditions for Agent-Ready Ops. Hit all four and the workflow is ready to run without you. Miss one and the automation will leak, usually as one email to the wrong contact.

proof_card.sample_top_leak: client-facing onboarding emails firing to the wrong contact (~6 hrs/week of cleanup plus the trust hit)

answers.label: Solo or under $1M revenue (1-9 people)
Boutique, $1M-$3M revenue (10-25 people)
Growing, $3M-$8M revenue (25-50 people)
Established, $8M-$20M revenue (50+ people)

questions.text: How consistently does your CRM workflow read structured fields instead of free-text notes?

answers.label: 1. It pulls key values out of free-text notes
2. Mostly notes, a few structured fields
3. Split between structured fields and notes
4. Mostly structured, one or two note-based reads left
5. Every field the workflow reads is structured

questions.text: How often are the fields your automation depends on actually required at intake?

answers.label: 1. All optional, they come back empty often
2. A couple are required, the rest optional
3. About half are required at intake
4. Most critical fields are required
5. Every field the workflow needs is required to submit

questions.text: How reliably do you confirm a contact or company record exists before the workflow fires?

answers.label: 1. We assume it exists, no check
2. We check sometimes, manually
3. We check, but no plan for an empty result
4. We check and have a fallback for misses
5. We verify the record and route empties to a human

questions.text: How clearly is each field mapped to a single source of truth across your tools?

answers.label: 1. Same value lives in 3+ tools, no winner
2. We know there is overlap but never resolved it
3. Some fields have a clear source, others do not
4. Most fields have one tool that wins
5. Every field maps to one source of truth

low.headline: Your inputs aren't ready to be trusted yet
low.text: The workflow is reading values it can't count on, which is how automations quietly grab the wrong field. Before any hands-off run, the data layer has to be the strong part of the build. Start by killing the free-text dependencies.
steps: List every field the workflow reads and flag which ones come from free-text notes
Make the fields the automation depends on required at intake so they stop coming back empty
Add a step that confirms the contact or company record exists and routes empties to a person

mid.headline: Inputs are half-trustworthy
mid.text: You have structure where it counts but a few soft spots will bite on edge cases. The gaps are usually optional fields you rely on and overlapping values across tools. Close those two and the input layer holds.
steps: Convert the last note-based reads into structured fields
Pick the winning tool for any value that lives in two places and document it
Define what the workflow does when a required field still arrives empty

high.headline: Input layer is solid
high.text: Your fields are structured, required, and traced to one source. Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Add validation that rejects malformed values before the workflow reads them
Monitor field-fill rates monthly so silent intake drift gets caught early
Document the data contract so a new hire can extend the workflow without breaking it

operator_brief.headline_number: ~1 in 5 automated runs misfires when a relied-on field is optional
operator_brief.lever: What I'd do: make every field the workflow depends on required at intake before touching the automation itself.
talking_points: Free-text notes are where the workflow grabs the wrong value, and we can't see it happen until a client does.
Optional fields we rely on come back empty often enough to break trust in the system.
One source of truth per field removes the guesswork about which tool is right.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Run the existing workflow in log-only mode for one week and count how many records had a missing or note-based field the automation needed.

questions.text: How completely are your routing rules written down before the workflow runs?

answers.label: 1. They live in one person's head
2. A rough idea exists, nothing written
3. The main rules are documented, edge cases are not
4. Most rules are written with examples
5. Every routing rule is documented at field-and-value level

questions.text: How well could someone other than you explain why a record gets routed the way it does?

answers.label: 1. Nobody else could explain it
2. One other person, vaguely
3. The team gets the gist, not the specifics
4. Most of the team can explain the common paths
5. Anyone on the team can trace any routing decision

questions.text: How precisely have you defined which deal or record types the workflow should skip entirely?

answers.label: 1. No skip rules, it processes everything
2. We have a vague sense of exceptions
3. A few skip cases are written down
4. Most exceptions are defined, new business handled separately
5. Every skip and exception case is documented and tested

low.headline: The logic isn't out of your head yet
low.text: If your best person can't explain how a record gets routed, the workflow can't encode it safely. Tacit rules have to become explicit before automation. Write the rules at the level of a real example, like the company name and the folder it should land in.
steps: Write each routing rule with a concrete example, field name and value included
Have a second person read the rules and try to predict where five real records go
List the deal and record types the workflow should skip entirely

mid.headline: Main paths are clear, edges are fuzzy
mid.text: Your common routing is documented well enough to run. The risk sits in the exceptions and the new-business versus existing-business split. Get those on paper and the logic is ready to hand to a system.
steps: Document the edge cases your team handles by instinct today
Separate new-business routing from existing-business routing explicitly
Test the documented rules against a month of real records before going live

high.headline: Decision logic is encodable
high.text: Your rules are written, explainable, and exception-aware. Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Version your rule doc so logic changes are tracked over time
Add a quarterly review where the team confirms the rules still match reality
Capture new edge cases as they appear instead of patching the workflow silently

operator_brief.headline_number: 100% of agent builds stall when routing logic lives only in one head
operator_brief.lever: What I'd do: write every routing rule at field-and-value level and have a second person predict outcomes before automating.
talking_points: If only one person can explain the routing, the workflow is a single point of failure.
New business and existing business usually need different logic, and skipping that split causes misroutes.
Documented skip rules stop the automation from touching records it was never meant to handle.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Take 10 recent records, write down where each should route by the rules on paper, then check whether your current workflow agrees.

questions.text: How narrow is the initial scope of what this workflow handles?

answers.label: 1. It tries to handle every case on day one
2. Broad scope with a few carve-outs
3. Focused on one process but many variants
4. One process, the common cases only
5. One decision in one workflow, rest routed out

questions.text: How well-tested is your fuzzy matching against real client-name variations?

answers.label: 1. No matching logic, exact only or none
2. Matching exists, never tested on real names
3. Tested on a handful of names
4. Tested broadly, similarity threshold set
5. Validated at 90%+ similarity against real variations

questions.text: How clearly have you separated new-business logic from existing-business logic?

answers.label: 1. Same path for both, no distinction
2. We know they differ but handle it manually
3. Partly split, some overlap remains
4. Mostly separate paths with clear triggers
5. Fully separate logic for new vs existing

low.headline: Too much scope, too little matching trust
low.text: Automations that try to handle every case break on case number three. A narrow first cut and tested matching are what make a hands-off run survivable. Pick one decision, get it right, then expand.
steps: Cut the workflow down to the single most common path and route everything else to a person
Build fuzzy matching and test it against real client-name variations from your CRM
Split new-business and existing-business records onto separate paths

mid.headline: Scope is reasonable, matching needs proof
mid.text: You have focused the workflow and started splitting record types. The open risk is matching accuracy on messy real-world names. Set a similarity threshold and prove it before trusting auto-matches.
steps: Test fuzzy matching against your real client list and aim for 90%+ similarity
Route any match below the threshold to human review
Tighten the new versus existing triggers so nothing falls between them

high.headline: Scope and matching are dialed
high.text: Narrow scope, tested matching, clean record-type split. Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Expand scope one case at a time, measuring error rate after each addition
Log low-confidence matches so you can tune the threshold with real data
Re-test matching whenever you onboard a batch of new clients

operator_brief.headline_number: auto-matching below a 90% similarity score is where wrong-record misfires start
operator_brief.lever: What I'd do: set a similarity threshold, route anything below it to a human, and keep the first scope to one decision.
talking_points: A workflow that handles every edge case on day one breaks fast and erodes trust in the whole build.
Fuzzy matching that hasn't been tested on real client-name variations will pair records incorrectly.
New and existing business need different handling, and one shared path is a misroute waiting to happen.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Run your matching logic against the full client list in test mode and review every match that scored under 90%.

questions.text: How consistently does a person review any output that reaches a client before it sends?

answers.label: 1. Client-facing sends fire fully automatically
2. Review happens only when someone remembers
3. Some client outputs are reviewed, others are not
4. Most client-facing sends pass a person first
5. Every client-facing output passes a person before it sends

questions.text: How clearly have you identified which steps touch a client directly versus internal-only steps?

answers.label: 1. We have never mapped this
2. We have a rough sense, nothing written
3. Documented for the main flow only
4. Most steps are tagged client-facing or internal
5. Every step is tagged and gated accordingly

questions.text: How well-defined is the approval gate for client-facing sends?

answers.label: 1. No gate exists
2. A vague who-checks-what with no owner
3. A gate exists but the trigger is unclear
4. Clear gate with a named owner for most cases
5. Defined gate, named owner, clear pass and reject paths

questions.text: How confident are you that a misfire cannot email the wrong contact?

answers.label: 1. It has already happened or easily could
2. Not confident, no safeguard in place
3. Somewhat, but no hard stop
4. Confident, a review catches most cases
5. A hard gate makes a wrong-contact send impossible

low.headline: Nothing stands between the system and a wrong send
low.text: This is the category that loses clients. The fastest way to lose one to automation is a single email firing to the wrong person. Until client-facing steps are gated, keep the approval on. Map what touches a client first.
steps: Tag every workflow step as client-facing or internal-only
Put a human approval gate on every client-facing send with a named owner
Add a hard stop that blocks the send if the contact match is below threshold

mid.headline: Gates exist but they leak
mid.text: You review some client outputs and have started mapping the flow. The gap is consistency and ownership. A gate that fires only when someone remembers is the same as no gate on a busy week. Name an owner and make the gate mandatory.
steps: Make the approval gate mandatory for every client-facing send, not optional
Assign a named owner so review never falls through on a busy week
Define the reject path so a flagged send has somewhere to go

high.headline: The wrong-person risk is contained
high.text: Client-facing steps are mapped, gated, and owned. The 15-20% routed to review is the design working, not a failure. Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Track approval-gate volume so you can spot when more cases become safe to auto-clear
Add confidence scoring so high-certainty sends clear faster and low-certainty ones escalate
Review rejected sends monthly to find logic gaps worth fixing upstream

operator_brief.headline_number: one wrong-contact email can cost a $10k+/mo retainer
operator_brief.lever: What I'd do: gate every client-facing send behind a named human owner before anything runs hands-off.
talking_points: Most CRM workflows are safe to run hands-off. The handful that touch a client directly are the ones that need a person in the loop.
A review that happens only when someone remembers fails on exactly the weeks we are busiest.
A hard stop on low-confidence contact matches makes the worst-case send impossible, not just unlikely.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Add a one-step approval queue for client-facing sends for two weeks and count how many you would have caught before they went out.

questions.text: How clearly have you defined what happens when enrichment or matching comes back empty?

answers.label: 1. Undefined, the workflow guesses or breaks
2. We deal with it after it breaks
3. Handled for the obvious cases only
4. Most empty results route somewhere safe
5. Every empty result has a defined fallback

questions.text: How quickly would you know if the workflow fired incorrectly?

answers.label: 1. Only when a client complains
2. Eventually, if someone notices
3. Within a few days on review
4. Same day via a check or alert
5. Immediately, an alert fires on failure

questions.text: How well do you log and review what the automation did on each run?

answers.label: 1. No logging, the run is a black box
2. Some logs exist, nobody reads them
3. Logged, reviewed only when something breaks
4. Logged and reviewed periodically
5. Every run is logged and reviewed on a set cadence

low.headline: You're flying blind on failure
low.text: A workflow you can't see is a workflow you can't trust to run alone. If you only learn about a misfire when a client complains, the damage is already done. Decide what happens on an empty result, then add visibility.
steps: Define a fallback for every empty enrichment or matching result
Add an alert that fires the moment the workflow fails or skips a step
Turn on run logging so every action the automation takes is recorded

mid.headline: You'd catch failures, just not fast
mid.text: You have logging and some handling, but the feedback loop is slow. The goal is to know within the same day, not the same week. Tighten alerting and set a review cadence so problems surface before a client does.
steps: Add same-day alerting on failed or skipped runs
Set a fixed cadence to review logs instead of only checking when something breaks
Confirm every empty-result path routes to a person rather than guessing

high.headline: The workflow is observable
high.text: Empty results are handled, failures alert fast, and runs get reviewed on a cadence. This is what hands-off-ready looks like. Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Add a weekly summary of what the automation did and what it routed out
Track misfire rate over time so you can prove the workflow is getting safer
Build a one-click rollback for the rare run that goes sideways

operator_brief.headline_number: knowing within the same day vs the same week is the difference between a fix and a lost client
operator_brief.lever: What I'd do: alert on failure in real time and give every empty result a defined fallback before going hands-off.
talking_points: If we only hear about a misfire when a client complains, the trust damage is already done.
An empty enrichment or match result needs a defined path, otherwise the workflow guesses and guesses wrong.
Logging every run is what lets us prove the automation is safe instead of hoping it is.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Wire a failure alert to Slack or email for one week and confirm you get notified before anyone downstream notices a problem.
